analysis.one_liner: Gives poor tenants lawyers in eviction cases and creates a national evictions database.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Banking Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Justice Department $125 million a year for five years to pay for lawyers for tenants facing eviction whose income is below 125% of the federal poverty level. It would also have required HUD to build a national database of evictions, tracking who gets evicted, who files the cases, and who has a lawyer, plus a government study on whether giving tenants lawyers changes outcomes. It was introduced by one senator, never gained a cosponsor, and was sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants facing eviction — people whose income is under 125% of the poverty line — would get a lawyer paid for by federal grants to their state or city. In eviction court, landlords almost always have attorneys and most tenants do not; free representation means tenants can raise defenses like code violations, avoid default judgments, and more often stay housed. The public also gains: a national eviction database would show, for the first time in one place, which landlords file the most evictions, how often tenants face court alone, and how evictions fall on tenants by race, family status, and disability.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $125 million a year for fiscal years 2024-2028 in Justice Department grants so states and cities can hire lawyers dedicated to representing tenants in eviction cases, with grants of at least $1 million sized to local eviction rates [S2][S3].
Limits eligibility to individuals whose income is below 125% of the federal poverty level, targeting aid to the poorest tenants rather than all renters [S2][S3].

Requires HUD to build a national database covering court-ordered, administrative, and illegal evictions, including data on landlords (units owned, attorneys, fees charged), tenants (race, family status, disability, whether they had counsel), and outcomes, with privacy safeguards for domestic violence survivors [S3].

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study how the legal system fails tenants in eviction cases, whether lawyers change outcomes and default rates, and the potential cost savings of providing representation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants — $125 million a year for the lawyer program plus $100 million a year for the database, authorized but subject to annual appropriations. Landlords would bear the practical cost: eviction cases against represented tenants take longer, face more defenses, and more often end with the tenant staying or paying less, and the database would make their eviction filing patterns publicly traceable. State courts would take on new data-reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: The program is a grant, not a guaranteed right: $125 million a year divided across every state and large city cannot cover all eligible tenants, and courts and cities could decline to apply, leaving coverage patchwork depending on where a tenant lives [S3].

The database requires state courts to collect and report detailed data on every eviction case — including judge names, tenant demographics, and landlord histories — a substantial administrative burden on clerks and courts, with $100 million a year authorized for the system itself [S3].

A good-faith cost objection: every dollar spent defending tenants is a dollar landlords may never collect, and slower eviction cases raise landlords' legal and carrying costs, which can be passed through to rent or discourage small landlords from renting at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well documented in policy research: tenants with lawyers are far less likely to lose their homes by default, and several cities that have tried right-to-counsel programs have kept families housed. The bill's design is honest — it targets the poorest tenants, funds lawyers directly, and pairs the program with data collection and a cost-benefit study. The main weaknesses are scale (grant funding covers a fraction of eligible tenants) and the heavy data-reporting load on state courts. On balance the benefits to low-income renters clearly outweigh the costs, which fall mostly on federal appropriations and on landlords who would face better-defended cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the Eviction Prevention Act on December 11, 2023; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners benefit because no lawyer program or public eviction database was created — eviction cases remain as they are, with most tenants unrepresented. State courts avoid the data-reporting burden, and federal taxpayers avoid the authorized $225 million a year, though none of it was ever appropriated.

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2023 and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee; no other senator signed on

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote, so it never reached the floor

against.name: No second senator
against.what_they_did: None of the 99 other senators signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor and no visible coalition to move it

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so party positions were never recorded; it had one Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of any party, and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Grant-funded lawyers for poor tenants would raise the cost and length of eviction cases and more often end with tenants staying or negotiating, and the database would publicly trace which landlords file the most evictions and what fees they charge. The bill died, so none of this took effect.

industries.industry: Landlord-tenant attorneys and legal aid organizations
industries.note: The bill would have funneled $125 million a year to states and cities to hire dedicated eviction-defense attorneys — new public funding for legal services lawyers. It died, so no funding was created.

industries.industry: State court systems and court clerks
industries.note: Courts would have gained federal data funding ($100 million a year) but taken on a detailed annual reporting duty covering every eviction case, including tenant demographics and judge names. The bill died, so no duties were imposed.
